title: The Seventy Years
lead: Jeremiah's prophecy that Babylon's rule, and Judah's desolation, would last seventy years. Later writers read it as the land's repayment of missed Sabbaths, counted it in different ways, and reinterpreted it as seventy weeks of years.

sections.h: The seventy years across the Bible
sections.b: Jeremiah foretold that the nations would serve Babylon seventy years, after which God would bring the exiles back (Jeremiah 25:11–12; Jeremiah 29:10). Chronicles links this with the warning of Leviticus that an exiled people's land would make up for its Sabbaths (Leviticus 26:34–35; 2 Chronicles 36:21). Zechariah, in 520 BC, speaks of God's anger "these seventy years" (Zechariah 1:12; Zechariah 7:5). Daniel reads Jeremiah's words and is told of seventy weeks, seventy sevens of years (Daniel 9:2; Daniel 9:24). Whether the number marks a precise span or a lifetime of judgment is debated. An inscription of Esarhaddon has Marduk write seventy years for Babylon's desolation and then turn the tablet over to make it eleven, which suggests seventy was a known term for divine anger.

sections.b: Daniel 9 turns Jeremiah's seventy years into seventy "weeks" of years, 490 years, ending in the cutting off of an anointed one and the end of sacrifice (Daniel 9:24–27). Traditional Christian readers count the weeks to the ministry and death of Christ. Most critical scholars, with John Collins, read them as pointing to the crisis under Antiochus IV in 167–164 BC. Rabbinic chronology counts them from the first temple's destruction to the second's in AD 70 (Seder Olam 28). The Talmud also works through Jeremiah's seventy years and shows Belshazzar and Ahasuerus miscounting them (Bavli Megillah 11b–12a). See the topic on Daniel.
